title: Singin' in the Rain
synopsis: A silent star, a starlet with a terrible voice, a chorus girl with talent, and the day the talkies arrived in Hollywood.

nodes.text: Searchlights rake the sky over Grauman's. A radio woman asks about your rise and you deliver the line you have said four hundred times — dignity, always dignity — while the truth stands two feet away in a rented tux, eating a canape. Cosmo knows every pool hall you were thrown out of. He is enjoying himself enormously.

choices.consequence: You give the radio audience a conservatory, a Shakespeare tour, and a European finishing school. Cosmo, three feet off, silently mouths the word Duluth at you.
You start to say pool hall and hear your own mouth produce preparatory academy instead. The mouth has been trained. The mouth wins.

nodes.text: Lina steps to the microphone in six pounds of beading and opens her mouth. The sound that comes out could strip varnish off a door. Two rows physically lean back. The studio spent nine years making sure this woman never spoke above a title card, and a microphone has undone all of it in four seconds.

choices.consequence: You tell her she was luminous. She agrees, at length, in that voice, for six full minutes, while you nod and quietly perish.
You duck behind a pillar, and R. F. finds you there and asks, with real warmth, why you are standing behind a pillar.

nodes.text: Cosmo plays the party like a man scoring a disaster in real time: minor key when Lina laughs, a little trill when the studio head crosses the room. He is the best musician on the lot and the lot has him doing sound effects for two-reel comedies. He has never once mentioned this.

choices.consequence: He tells you the talkies are coming and you had better learn to talk. You laugh. He does not laugh, which is new.
You wave him off and go find a drink. Behind you the piano switches, pointedly, into a funeral march in three-quarter time.

nodes.text: You land in a stranger's convertible with a fan still holding your sleeve, and the stranger informs you that you are not an actor, you are a shadow on a wall doing pantomime. Then she says her name is Kathy Selden and that she works in the theater. Real theater. She lets the word sit there.

choices.consequence: You concede the point about shadows. She does not soften an inch; she just files it away, which is somehow both worse and better.
You get her name, her profession, and a look suggesting she would have preferred the streetcar. You are absolutely going to find her again.

nodes.text: The microphone hides in a bouquet on Lina's shoulder. Every time she turns her head the dialogue vanishes; every time she turns back it returns at cannon volume. Then a grip in the third row sneezes, and the sound man reports, without any expression at all, that the sneeze is the best-recorded performance on the stage.

choices.consequence: You chalk an X on the floor and beg her to keep her chin above it. She hits it twice out of nine takes and calls that collaboration.
You take it out on a kid in headphones who did nothing to anybody. He apologizes to you. You feel roughly two inches tall for an hour.

nodes.text: The rival studio's talking picture sells out for a week straight, and R. F. Simpson makes an announcement to a soundstage of people who cannot hear him over their own panic. The Dueling Cavalier will talk. Nobody asks the obvious question about Lina. Every person in that room is thinking it, in perfect silence.

choices.consequence: You sign up for the first diction class on the lot, which guarantees you will be the first person publicly terrible at something new.
You call the whole thing a fad in front of six witnesses. That reel of you saying it will follow you around for years.

nodes.text: Moses supposes. The instructor holds a tape ruler under your jaw and asks for rounder vowels while Cosmo, uninvited, starts a rhythm from the corner of the room. Ninety seconds later there are two grown men tap dancing on a desk and an elocution coach flat on his back with a mouth chart on his chest.

choices.consequence: You turn the drill into a number and learn more in four minutes than in a week of it. The coach files a written complaint about his furniture.
You do it properly, flatly, correctly. Cosmo mimes falling asleep and then genuinely falls asleep, which was not part of the bit.

nodes.text: Publicity decides Lina's voice is now a studio asset to be protected, like the negative. No interviews. No radio. A man from the front office is assigned to stand near her at parties and answer questions on her behalf, cheerfully, in the third person, while she smiles and holds a glass she never drinks from.

choices.consequence: You cover for her at three luncheons and hate the taste of it. She never thanks you once; she assumes covering is simply part of your contract.
You tell Kathy the whole thing over a cold sandwich at midnight and feel lighter than you have since the premiere. Also, now two people know.

nodes.text: Cosmo's idea arrives fully formed at one in the morning: Kathy sings, Lina moves her mouth, the picture is saved. It is a good idea and a bad idea wearing the same hat. Kathy points out, evenly, that she would be handing her voice to the woman who had her fired off a lot.

choices.consequence: You promise it is temporary, one picture, that is all. You believe it while you are saying it, and that is the part you will think about later.
You tell Cosmo no. He sits at the piano and plays nothing at all for a full minute, which, from Cosmo, is a scream.

nodes.text: The sound drifts six frames and the entire house turns on you. Lina's line arrives before her lips move. Then the reels flip and she is speaking in your voice while you speak in hers, and eight hundred people in Pasadena laugh so hard that a man drops his hat and never picks it up.

choices.consequence: You stay through the credits with a pencil, writing down every laugh and exactly where it came from. It is the worst homework of your life.
You are in the alley before the second reel ends, tie loose, breathing like you sprinted. Cosmo brings your hat out about ten minutes later.

nodes.text: Three in the morning in the cutting room, one moviola and one bottle. Cosmo says the picture does not need dialogue, it needs songs. Call it The Dancing Cavalier, cut in a modern number, blame the whole thing on a dream sequence. Kathy is already sketching costumes on the back of a call sheet.

choices.consequence: You say yes at 3:40 in the morning. By breakfast you have a title, a running order, and absolutely no plan for telling the front office.
You say it cannot be saved and go home. Cosmo keeps working anyway, alone, until the light in the window turns gray.

nodes.text: The Broadway Melody sequence takes fourteen days and costs more than the rest of the picture combined. Sequins, a fog machine, a girl with a coin flip and a cigarette holder, and a scarf that is somehow twenty yards long. You describe all of it to R. F. in his office. He says he cannot quite visualize it.

choices.consequence: You dance it yourself for fourteen days and lose nine pounds doing it. On day twelve the scarf wraps your whole face and you keep going.
You hand the number to a younger hoofer and watch from the flies. He is terrific. You are relieved and jealous in roughly equal measure.

nodes.text: Lina has read her contract. Lina has a lawyer now. She stands in R. F.'s office with a fingernail on page nine and explains that publicity approval means everything, that Kathy's name appears nowhere, and that she can shut the picture down before lunch. She is, infuriatingly, correct on all three counts.

choices.consequence: You tell her no in front of her own lawyer. She smiles like a hood ornament and has your dressing room reassigned by Thursday morning.
You give her the credit line and tell yourself it is one picture. Kathy learns about it from a trade paper instead of from you.

nodes.text: Kathy's porch light goes out behind you and the rain arrives all at once. You send the car away. Somewhere between the second lamppost and the third, the umbrella stops being weather protection and becomes a partner, and a beat cop watches a grown man in evening clothes stamp in a gutter with his face turned up.

choices.consequence: You sing the whole thing to an empty street and one baffled patrolman, and hand him the umbrella at the end because you no longer require it.
You keep it to a hum and a stride slightly too long for the block. The cop looks anyway. The song stays in your chest until morning.

nodes.text: She is gone before the last setup is struck. No note, no goodbye, just a coat missing from its hook and a dubbing schedule squared neatly on the table. The studio has already loaned her voice to Lina for two more pictures, and she signed the thing herself. That is the part that stops you cold.

choices.consequence: You reach the parking lot as her bus pulls out and run half a block in tap shoes. Every soul on the lot sees you do it.
You go back inside and work the rest of the day like a professional. It takes seven hours and you remember none of them.

nodes.text: Cosmo finds you on a dark stage with a piano and no audience and starts a song whose entire argument is agreement. You do the number for one stagehand, a push broom, and a fire bucket. The stagehand applauds with real feeling. It is the best crowd either of you has played to in months.

choices.consequence: You take the harmony and the two of you finish flat on your backs on the stage floor, wheezing, roughly twenty years old again.
You let him do it alone and watch from the bench. He plays to you like you are a sold-out house, because to him you are.

nodes.text: Second premiere, same searchlights, entirely different sweat. The Dancing Cavalier plays to a packed house and the house laughs where it is supposed to, a sound you had forgotten could be pleasant. Kathy is up in the projection booth. Lina is front row, waving at people who believe she talks like that.

choices.consequence: You hold a smile through two thousand feet of your own face and check the exit only twice. Nobody in the row can see your hands.
You go through a collar and a handkerchief before the second reel. Cosmo passes you a fresh one without taking his eyes off the screen.

nodes.text: The house is on its feet. Somebody calls for a speech, somebody else calls for a song, and the call becomes a chant, and Lina turns and looks at you with genuine fear for the first time since you have known her. Then she decides, out loud, to her lawyer, that Kathy will sing behind the curtain.

choices.consequence: You catch R. F.'s eye and the two of you agree to something without a word passing between you. Cosmo is already halfway up the rope.
You step toward the microphone to take it for her. She puts out one hand and stops you, because she wants the applause more than the rescue.

nodes.text: Kathy stands at the second microphone in the dark behind the screen, headphones on, watching a cue light. She thinks she is doing one last favor for a picture she likes. Above her, three men are quietly untying a rope. You have perhaps forty seconds to decide whether she gets to know what happens next.

choices.consequence: You get to her and say two sentences. She looks at you, then at the curtain, then nods once and sings it anyway.
You leave her in the dark with her cue light and let the reveal happen to her instead of with her. She forgives you. It takes a while.

nodes.text: The curtain rises on a girl in a plain dress singing into a microphone, and Lina keeps mouthing the words for four entire seconds before she understands why the room sounds the way it does. A thousand faces do the arithmetic at once. Somebody up in the balcony starts laughing and cannot stop.

choices.consequence: You take the microphone and give two thousand people the name of the girl currently running for the exit. Then you make them all say it back.
You stay in the wings and let it happen without you, so Kathy carries the entire thing alone, and she does it beautifully, and you notice.

nodes.text: Six weeks on, there is a billboard over Sunset the size of a house: your name, her name, an umbrella between you, and SINGIN IN THE RAIN in letters eight feet high. Kathy stands underneath it eating an orange and says the painter got your chin wrong, and she is right about that.

choices.consequence: You kiss her on a public sidewalk under a forty-foot version of yourselves while a tour bus slows down to look, and neither of you minds at all.
You just stand there looking up at it. She takes your hand by the wrist, the way people do when the other hand has an orange in it.
Cosmo pulls up honking, hangs out the window, and asks whether either of you noticed his name is also on that poster, small, at the very bottom.

nodes.text: You spin the umbrella at the curb, hand it off to a patrolman who has given up on you entirely, and stamp through the gutter with your face turned straight up into the weather. Traffic waits. A woman with grocery bags watches from a doorway and decides not to interrupt. Fifty years from now, people not yet born will do a bad version of this in their kitchens, and every one of them will be happy doing it.

Her name goes above the title in letters that cost the studio one very loud argument. Lina gets a vocal coach three hours a day in a bungalow at the far end of the lot, and by 1932 she can order lunch without alarming a waiter. Kathy's new contract has two clauses about billing and one, which she insisted on personally, guaranteeing a full hour to eat.

Cosmo gets a picture of his own, which he directs badly and scores brilliantly, and the commissary names a sandwich after him: turkey, slaw, and a third component nobody has ever identified. He eats one every Friday for thirty years and complains about it every single time. On the wall behind the register hangs a photograph of three people standing in the rain, and he is in it.
